Winter Riding by Region

Winter riding in the UK is about choosing the mildest, lowest-risk locations. Forget mountain passes and Highland single-track roads. Focus on low-level, sheltered routes in the warmest corners of Britain. Here's where to ride from December to February.

The Warmest Options

  • Cornwall and Devon (★★★★): The mildest region in winter. Temperatures rarely drop below 5°C near the coast. Coastal rides on dry days can be genuinely pleasant. The Gulf Stream keeps the southwest notably warmer than the rest of England.
  • South Wales Coast (★★★): The Gower and Pembrokeshire coast are milder than inland Wales. Sheltered valleys offer protected riding.
  • South Coast (★★★): Dorset, Hampshire, and Sussex are mild and low-lying. Gentle rides through the New Forest and along the coast are achievable.

Acceptable with Preparation

  • Cotswolds (★★★): Low-level, sheltered riding through villages. Short rides between warm pubs are the winter touring ideal.
  • East Anglia (★★★): Dry (the driest region in winter), flat, and low-level. Big skies and empty lanes.
  • Welsh Valleys (★★): Sheltered valley roads are rideable. Avoid anything above 300m.

Not Recommended

  • Scottish Highlands (★): Snow, ice, frozen roads, and minimal daylight (under 7 hours). Mountain passes close.
  • Lake District (★★): Cold and wet. The passes are often icy. Valley roads only, and with full winter gear.
  • North Pennines (★): Among the coldest, most exposed roads in England. Not for winter riding.

Winter Riding Rules

  • Stick to main roads that are gritted
  • Ride between 10am and 2pm for the warmest window
  • Never ride if temperature is below 2°C — ice risk is too high
  • Keep rides short (30-60 miles) and purposeful
  • Tell someone where you're going and when you'll be back
Winter riding isn't about epic mileage or bucket-list destinations. It's about maintaining your connection to motorcycling through the darkest months. A 40-mile ride to a warm pub in Cornwall on a dry December day feeds the soul until spring returns.

Making the Most of Winter

Winter riding is about quality over quantity. A 40-mile ride on a crisp, dry December day — with frost on the fields, clear blue sky, and not another soul on the road — can be more memorable than a 200-mile summer blast in traffic. The key is choosing your days carefully and matching your expectations to the conditions.

Keep your bike ready to ride at short notice. When a dry, mild winter day appears in the forecast, you want to be able to grab it without spending the morning doing maintenance. A pre-winter service, ongoing chain lubrication, and a trickle charger keeping the battery healthy mean your bike is always ready when the weather window opens.

Winter is also the time to invest in skills development. Advanced riding courses run year-round, and the reduced traffic makes winter an excellent time to practice techniques. The skills you develop in challenging winter conditions will serve you well when the easier months return. Read our What to Ride in Summer: UK Regions Ranked for June-August Touring guide for more. faq.q: Where is the mildest winter riding in the UK?
faq.a: Cornwall and Devon. The Gulf Stream keeps the southwest notably warmer than the rest of England, and coastal temperatures rarely drop below 5C, so dry-day coastal rides can be genuinely pleasant. The south Wales coast and the south coast of England are the next best options.

faq.q: When should I ride on a winter day?
faq.a: Between 10am and 2pm, the warmest window when any overnight ice has had the best chance to clear from gritted roads. Never ride if the temperature is below 2C, as ice risk becomes too high. Keep rides short and purposeful, typically 30 to 60 miles, and stick to main roads that are gritted.

faq.q: Which regions should I avoid in winter?
faq.a: The Scottish Highlands, with snow, ice, frozen roads, and under seven hours of daylight, plus closed mountain passes. The North Pennines are among the coldest, most exposed roads in England. The Lake District is cold and wet with icy passes; if you go, use valley roads only and full winter gear.

faq.q: How do I keep my bike ready for winter riding?
faq.a: Keep it ready to grab a dry-day window at short notice. A pre-winter service, ongoing chain lubrication, and a trickle charger keeping the battery healthy mean you are not spending the morning on maintenance when a rare mild, dry day appears. Winter is quality over quantity, so being ready lets you seize the good days.
